225.title: What she hath done (Mark 14:1–11)
225.hook: the anointing at Bethany: what she did will be told wherever the gospel is preached
225.howItsDone: The Church reads the anointing at Bethany during Holy Week, and Catholic bishops bless the holy oils at the Chrism Mass that same week, the oils used for anointing at baptism, confirmation, ordination and for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one word from the Mount of Olives: watch. Your line was finish today as if it matters. When did you catch yourself on autopilot? Today the passion begins, with a woman who was wide awake. Day two hundred twenty-five.

It's two days before Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes are looking for a quiet way to arrest Jesus and put him to death. Not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot. Meanwhile, just over the hill in the village of Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of a man called Simon the leper. A woman walks in holding an alabaster jar of perfume, pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't open it. She breaks it. And she pours it over his head. The room fills with the smell, and with outrage.
screen: `TWO DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `A DINNER IN BETHANY.` → `SHE BREAKS THE JAR.`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. Some at the table are indignant. What a waste. That could have been sold for more than three hundred pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and given to the poor. It sounds reasonable. It sounds even holy. Second, Jesus defends her. In the Douay-Rheims: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." You'll always have the poor with you, he says, and you can do them good whenever you want. You won't always have me. Then: "She hath done what she could: she is come beforehand to anoint my body for the burial." She seems to understand what the disciples still don't: he's going to die. Third, the anointing itself. Remember, Christ means the anointed one. In the old story, Samuel pours oil on Saul's head to make him king. Here, in a friend's house, a woman whose name Mark never tells us pours oil on Jesus's head. Not a priest. Not an apostle. Her. Fourth, the promise: "wheresoever this gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she hath done, shall be told for a memory of her." And here it is, told again, in your ears. Then look what Mark puts right next to her. Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand Jesus over, and they promise him money. She's unnamed, and remembered for pouring out something precious. He's named, and he's selling someone precious. John's Gospel tells a similar anointing and names the woman Mary of Bethany. Mark lets her stay nameless, and remembered anyway.
screen: `WHAT A WASTE, THEY SAY.` · `LET HER ALONE: A GOOD WORK.` · `SHE ANOINTS THE ANOINTED ONE.` · `TOLD WHEREVER THE GOSPEL GOES.` · then, large: `SHE HATH DONE WHAT SHE COULD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone's kindness to another. Settle and breathe. Think of someone who did something good that nobody noticed. A coworker who covered for you. A neighbor who shoveled your walk. A grandparent who quietly held a family together. Let their face come to mind, and remember exactly what they did. Now decide who you'll tell about it today, so it's told for a memory of them. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Memory. The promise Jesus makes about the woman who broke the jar at Bethany: wherever the gospel is preached, this will be told for a memory of her. Today's word.
Your line: she did what she could. Today, do the one generous thing in front of you, even if someone calls it a waste. Day two hundred twenty-five.

Mark never names her. John's Gospel tells a similar anointing by Mary of Bethany.

fork.setup: you're at the table in Bethany. a woman breaks a jar of costly perfume over his head. someone says it should have been sold for the poor. what does Jesus say?
options: they're right; next time, sell it.
let her alone. she has done a good thing.
fork.reveal: "Let her alone, why do you molest her? She hath wrought a good work upon me." and she will be remembered wherever the gospel goes.

original.note: Greek: a memorial, a remembrance. told for a memory of her.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman wasted expensive perfume.
what it means: she anoints the anointed one for burial, understanding what the disciples don't, and is remembered wherever the gospel goes.
what a scholar hears: a Markan sandwich, the plot, the anointing, Judas: an unnamed woman's gift framed by a named man's betrayal.

226.title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–31)
226.hook: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the new testament
226.howItsDone: At every Catholic Mass the priest repeats Jesus's words over the bread and wine at the consecration, and Catholics receive Communion believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ; the Last Supper is remembered especially on Holy Thursday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, memory: a woman broke a jar of perfume over Jesus's head, and he said she did what she could. Your line was she did what she could. Whose kindness did you tell? Today, supper. Day two hundred twenty-six.

It's the first day of the feast of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lambs are sacrificed. The disciples ask where they should get the meal ready. Jesus sends two of them into the city with odd directions: you'll meet a man carrying a jar of water. Follow him. Wherever he goes in, ask the owner for the guest room. He'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. It all happens just as he said. That evening he arrives with the twelve. Catholics trace every Mass back to what happens at this table.
screen: `THE DAY OF THE PASSOVER LAMBS.` → `FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM, READY.`

segments.voice: First, the betrayal at the table. While they're reclining and eating, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "one of you that eateth with me shall betray me." They're heartbroken, and one by one they ask him: "Is it I?" Nobody points at anyone else. Each one wonders about himself. Second, the bread. "And whilst they were eating, Jesus took bread; and blessing, broke, and gave to them, and said: Take ye. This is my body." Took, blessed, broke, gave. Mark used almost the same four actions at the two feedings in the wilderness, and some readers hear those baskets echo here. Third, the cup. He takes a cup, gives thanks, and they all drink from it. Then he says: "This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many." Testament here means covenant, a binding promise. At Sinai, Moses sealed God's covenant with blood. Now Jesus speaks of his own. Fourth, what Catholics believe. The Catholic Church teaches that at every Mass, when the priest speaks these words over bread and wine, they truly become the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine. The Church calls this transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also believe in a real change, and speak of it as a mystery; many Protestants understand the meal as a memorial or a spiritual presence. And notice the first word over the bread: take. In Mark, the bread is given to be received. Then they sing a hymn and walk out to the Mount of Olives, and Peter promises: "Although all shall be scandalized in thee, yet not I." Before the cock crows twice, Jesus tells him, you'll deny me three times.
screen: `ONE OF YOU WILL BETRAY ME. IS IT I?` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · `THE BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT.` · `CATHOLICS TRACE EVERY MASS HERE.` · then, large: `TAKE YE. THIS IS MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember the last supper at your next meal. Right now, settle and breathe, and picture that room. Low tables, lamplight, thirteen people close together, the smell of bread. Now picture your next meal, wherever it will be. Decide that before you eat it, you'll pause for one breath and remember this table. If you pray, you can say grace, or simply say thank you. If you don't, just notice the bread in your hands and who made it. The bell holds the time.
Transubstantiation. What Catholics believe happens at Mass when the priest repeats Jesus's words over bread and wine: they truly become his body and blood. Today's word.
Your line: take. Today, when something is offered, a meal, a hand, some help, don't refuse it. Take it, and say thank you. Day two hundred twenty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus's last meal before he died.
what it means: bread and cup given as his body and blood, a new covenant, the table every Mass goes back to.

227.title: Abba (Mark 14:32–52)
227.hook: he calls God by the family word, and a young man flees leaving his linen cloth
227.howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night many Catholic parishes keep watch before the Blessed Sacrament until midnight, remembering Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, and the Agony in the Garden is the first Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, transubstantiation: bread and cup, and one word, take. Your line was take. What did you accept without refusing? After supper they walked out to the Mount of Olives. Today, the garden. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

Most of us have had one night we'd never want to live again. Waiting for a phone call. Sitting by a bed. Today is that night for Jesus. They come to a place called Gethsemane, an olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives. The name probably means oil press. He tells most of the disciples to sit and wait, takes Peter, James and John further in, and Mark says he began to be terrified and deeply troubled. He tells them his soul is sorrowful even unto death. Stay here and watch. Then he goes a little further alone, and falls on the ground.
screen: `THE WORST NIGHT.` → `GETHSEMANE: THE OIL PRESS.` → `HE FALLS ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Face down in the dirt, he prays, in the Douay-Rheims: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee: remove this chalice from me; but not what I will, but what thou wilt." Abba is Aramaic, the everyday word for father used inside a family. Mark keeps the sound, then translates it. You'll sometimes hear that abba means daddy. Scholars now say that's too cute: grown children called their fathers abba too. It's not baby talk. It's close, trusting, family speech, at the worst moment of his life. Second, the honesty. He asks for the cup to pass. He doesn't pretend to want it. And then he hands the choice back: not my will, yours. Catholics see here both his true human fear and his free obedience. Third, the sleepers. He comes back three times and finds them asleep. Remember the last word of his speech two days ago: watch. "Watch ye, and pray that you enter not into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Fourth, the arrest. Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and greets Jesus with a kiss. Someone draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. And then, Mark says, they all left him and fled. One more detail that only Mark tells. A young man was following, wearing only a linen cloth. They grab him, and he leaves the cloth in their hands and runs away naked. Nobody knows who he was. An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his Gospel. The sources don't say.
screen: `ABBA: THE FAMILY WORD FOR FATHER.` · `REMOVE THIS CHALICE. NOT MY WILL.` · `ASLEEP THREE TIMES. WATCH AND PRAY.` · `A KISS, A SWORD, AND THEY ALL FLED.` · then, large: `ABBA, FATHER, ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray to God as Abba, or sit with the word. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind the thing you most wish would pass from you right now. Say honestly that you don't want it. Then, if you pray, you can use Jesus's own words: Abba, Father. Just those two, slowly, on your breath, as many times as you need. If you don't pray, think of the person whose voice feels most like home, and let yourself rest in that for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Aramaic for father, the word used inside a family. Jesus says it face down in Gethsemane, the night before he dies. Today's word.
Your line: abba, father. Today, when you're afraid of something, say it honestly first, to God or to someone you trust, before you pretend you're fine. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Before the cock crows twice (Mark 14:53–72)
228.hook: Jesus is silent before the council; Peter weeps
228.howItsDone: Catholics bring their sins to the sacrament of confession, and Peter's denial and tears are often held up in Catholic preaching as a picture of sorrow that leads back to mercy rather than despair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba: Jesus face down in the garden, calling God by the family word. Your line was abba, father. What fear did you say out loud? After the arrest, everyone fled. Almost everyone. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

Three denials, spoken by a fire in the dark. Each one is said to protect himself, by the man who swore, only hours before, that he would never fall away. They take Jesus to the high priest's house, in the middle of the night, where the chief priests and elders gather. And Peter, who ran away with the others, comes back. He follows at a distance, right into the courtyard, and sits with the servants, warming himself by the fire. Two scenes are happening at once. Upstairs, a trial. Downstairs, by the fire, another one.
screen: `THREE DENIALS BY A FIRE.` → `PETER FOLLOWS AT A DISTANCE.` → `TWO TRIALS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. Inside, witnesses accuse Jesus, but their stories don't agree. The high priest stands up and demands an answer. In the Douay-Rheims: "But he held his peace, and answered nothing." Jesus, who's been talking all through Mark, now says nothing to the accusations. Second, the answer. The high priest asks him straight: are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed? And here, with no hedging at all, Jesus says it plainly: "I am." You shall see the Son of man at the right hand of power. It's called blasphemy, and some begin to spit on him and strike him. Third, the fire. Downstairs, a servant girl looks at Peter in the firelight: you were with the Nazarene. He says he doesn't know what she means. She tells the others. He denies it again. Then the bystanders say: surely you're one of them. You're a Galilean. And Peter begins to curse and swear: "I know not this man of whom you speak." Upstairs, Jesus says I am. Downstairs, Peter says I'm not. Fourth, the tears. "And immediately the cock crew again." Peter remembers the word, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt thrice deny me. "And he began to weep." One more thing. An early tradition, from a bishop named Papias, says Mark wrote down what Peter preached. If that's right, this story most likely came from Peter's own mouth. The man Catholics call the first pope told it on himself, and the Gospel kept it.
screen: `HE HELD HIS PEACE.` · `ARE YOU THE CHRIST? I AM.` · `BY THE FIRE: I KNOW NOT THIS MAN.` · `THE COCK CROWS, AND PETER WEEPS.` · then, large: `AND HE BEGAN TO WEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself be sorry. Settle and breathe. Bring back one moment you've regretted, when you protected yourself and someone else paid for it. Don't relive it in detail. Don't defend yourself. Just remember it, the way Peter remembered the word. If there are tears, let them come. If there aren't, let there be quiet. Being sorry is not the same as being finished. Peter's story didn't end by the fire. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God. The bell holds the time.
Blasphemy. What the high priest calls it when Jesus answers the elders plainly, I am, just before Peter, downstairs, denies him three times. Today's word.
Your line: peter wept. Today, if you owe someone an apology, even an old one, let this be the day you start it. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

Papias, an early bishop, says so, which would mean Peter told this story on himself.

I don't know what you mean.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter failed.
what it means: while Jesus says I am upstairs, Peter says I'm not downstairs, and then weeps. and it isn't the end of his story.
what a scholar hears: a Markan sandwich of two trials; eklaien, imperfect, 'kept weeping'; and Papias's tradition that Peter was Mark's source.

229.title: The crown (Mark 15:1–20)
229.hook: Barabbas released, the purple cloak, the crown of thorns
229.howItsDone: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns as the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the Church's corporal works of mercy, carried out through prison ministries in many dioceses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blasphemy: Jesus silent before the council, Peter by the fire. Your line was peter wept. Did you start an apology? Now it's morning, and Jesus is handed to Rome. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

Early in the morning, the chief priests, the elders and the scribes hold a council, bind Jesus, and hand him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. The sentence will be his to give. Pilate has a custom at the feast: he releases one prisoner, whoever the crowd asks for. In his jail right now is a man named Barabbas, locked up with rebels who committed murder in an uprising. So Pilate offers the crowd a choice. Jesus, or Barabbas. And before long, soldiers will put a crown on Jesus's head. Not gold.
screen: `HANDED OVER TO PILATE.` → `JESUS, OR BARABBAS?` → `A CROWN, NOT OF GOLD.`

segments.voice: First, Pilate's question. He asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Art thou the king of the Jews?" And Jesus answers: "Thou sayest it." Then he's silent again, while the chief priests accuse him of many things, and Pilate marvels. Second, the choice. Pilate seems to see that the charge comes out of envy. But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas. What shall I do with this king, then? Crucify him. And Pilate, wanting to satisfy the crowd, releases Barabbas, has Jesus scourged, and hands him over to be crucified. Some readers hear something in the prisoner's name. Barabbas can be heard as bar abba, Aramaic for son of the father, and last night Jesus called God Abba. If that's right, one son of the father walks free this morning, and the other takes his place. Third, the crown. Roman soldiers lead him into the governor's palace and call together the whole cohort. "And they clothe him with purple, and platting a crown of thorns, they put it upon him. And they began to salute him: Hail, king of the Jews." Purple is a king's color, and that's the joke. They hit his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. Fourth, the irony. Every piece of the mockery is true, in Mark's telling. They mean it as a joke: a purple cloak, a crown, a salute, kneeling soldiers. Mark's readers know he really is the king. The soldiers are acting out a coronation without knowing it. Catholics remember this scene in the rosary, the third Sorrowful Mystery, the crowning with thorns. It was Rome's soldiers who mocked him, and Rome that crucified him.
screen: `ART THOU THE KING? THOU SAYEST IT.` · `JESUS, OR BARABBAS?` · `PURPLE, THORNS, HAIL, KING.` · `A CORONATION THEY DON'T UNDERSTAND.` · then, large: `AND PLATTING A CROWN OF THORNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for prisoners, or hold them in mind. Settle and breathe. Jesus was a prisoner that morning: bound, mocked, beaten, with no one to speak for him. Right now, people are sitting in prison cells, some guilty, some not, some forgotten by everyone. Bring one to mind, if you know one. If you don't, picture a cell, and someone sitting in it this morning. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the people who guard them. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The crown. The crown of thorns Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus's head as a joke, while they hailed him as king. Today's word.
Your line: they mocked the king. Today, when you hear someone being mocked, in person or online, don't join in, and if you can, quietly take their side. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

230.title: Truly this man (Mark 15:21–47)
230.hook: Simon carries the cross, the centurion says Indeed this man was the son of God
230.tomorrow: Camp 4 close: he goes before you
230.howItsDone: Catholics walk the fourteen Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, where Simon of Cyrene helps Jesus carry the cross at the fifth station, and on Good Friday the passion is read aloud and the faithful venerate the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown: purple, thorns, and soldiers kneeling in mockery. Your line was they mocked the king. Whose side did you take? Today, one of those soldiers sees something. Day two hundred thirty.

A man is coming in from the countryside, passing by on the road. His name is Simon, from Cyrene, in North Africa. Roman soldiers grab him out of the crowd and force him to carry a condemned man's cross. Mark adds that he was the father of Alexander and Rufus, as if his first readers knew those two by name. Maybe they did. Maybe carrying that cross changed a family. And at the end of the road, at the place called Golgotha, the place of the skull, a Roman officer will say the sentence Mark has been building toward since his first line.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE, GRABBED.` → `THE FATHER OF ALEXANDER AND RUFUS.` → `GOLGOTHA, THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.`

segments.voice: First, the cross. They crucify him at the third hour, between two thieves. Over him, the charge: the King of the Jews. Passersby, priests and even the men crucified beside him mock him: he saved others, himself he cannot save. They're right, in a way they don't understand. Second, the cry. From the sixth hour darkness covers the land until the ninth. Then Jesus cries out in Aramaic, and Mark keeps the words: "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani? Which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Back in camp four, this path spent a day on that psalm. Jesus is praying the first line of Psalm 21 in the Douay, 22 in most Bibles, a psalm that begins in abandonment and ends in praise. With a loud cry, he dies. The veil of the Temple is torn in two, top to bottom. Third, the soldier. Mark began his Gospel calling Jesus the Son of God. A voice from heaven has said it. Demons have shouted it. But in Mark, no human being has said it and meant it, until now. The centurion standing facing the cross sees how he died, and says: "Indeed this man was the son of God." A Roman. A Gentile. The officer in charge of the execution. Fourth, who stayed. The men have all fled. But women were watching from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. Then Joseph of Arimathea, a respected council member, goes boldly to Pilate, asks for the body, wraps it in linen, lays it in a tomb cut from rock, and rolls a stone across the door.
screen: `HE SAVED OTHERS, HIMSELF HE CANNOT.` · `MY GOD, MY GOD: PSALM 21 [22].` · `A ROMAN SOLDIER SAYS IT.` · `THE WOMEN STAYED.` · then, large: `INDEED THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help carry someone's load. Settle and breathe. Simon didn't choose that cross. It was put on his shoulders on an ordinary day. Think of someone near you carrying something heavy right now. An illness, a move, a sick parent, a lot of work, a grief. Picture them. What's one piece of it you could carry for a while? A meal, an errand, an hour, a text that says I'm thinking of you. Decide on one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Centurion. The Roman officer at the cross who says, indeed this man was the son of God: the first human being in Mark to say it and mean it. Today's word.
Your line: the soldier saw. Today, look again at someone you've already decided about. You might see something you missed. Day two hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 230 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 4 CLOSE: HE GOES BEFORE YOU.`

231.title: Camp 4 close: he goes before you (Mark 16)
231.hook: the women at the tomb hear he goes before you into Galilee
231.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the resurrection at the Easter Vigil and on every Sunday, and the resurrection is the first Glorious Mystery of the rosary; Mark 16 is read at the Easter Vigil in the year of Mark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, centurion: a Roman soldier at the cross said indeed this man was the son of God. Your line was the soldier saw. Who did you look at again? Today the camp ends, at an empty tomb. Day two hundred thirty-one.

Very early on the first day of the week, with the sun now risen, three women walk to the tomb with spices to anoint the body: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They had watched the crucifixion from a distance. On the way they worry about something practical: who will roll the stone away for us? It was very big. They're not expecting a miracle. They're expecting a heavy rock and a dead friend. Then they look up, and the stone is already rolled back.
screen: `SUNRISE, THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` → `WHO WILL ROLL THE STONE AWAY?` → `IT'S ALREADY ROLLED BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the news. Inside, a young man in a white robe is sitting on the right, and they're terrified. He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be not affrighted; you seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified: he is risen, he is not here." Second, the errand: "But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he goeth before you into Galilee; there you shall see him, as he told you." And Peter. The one who wept by the fire is named on purpose. Not left out. And Galilee is where it all began: the lake, the boats, the ordinary towns. He's not waiting in the Temple. He's gone ahead, back to the everyday. Third, the ending. The women run from the tomb, trembling, "and they said nothing to any man; for they were afraid." In some of the oldest manuscripts we have, Mark stops right there. Later manuscripts carry a longer ending, with the risen Jesus appearing first to Mary Magdalene, and sending the eleven out to the whole world. The Catholic Church receives that longer ending as inspired Scripture, and scholars still debate who wrote it and when. Either way, the story didn't stay untold. You're hearing it. Fourth, look back. This camp was the text itself. The Psalms: two ways, the Lord ruleth me, be still, have mercy, out of the depths, let every spirit praise. Then Mark straight through: the beginning, fishers of men, the sower, peace be still, Ephphatha, who do you say I am, Bartimaeus, the widow's mites, Abba, truly this man. And now, he goes before you. Tomorrow a new camp begins, the depths, starting with how Catholics pray when words run out.
screen: `HE IS RISEN, HE IS NOT HERE.` · `TELL HIS DISCIPLES, AND PETER.` · `THEY SAID NOTHING; THEY WERE AFRAID.` · `THE PSALMS, THEN MARK STRAIGHT THROUGH.` · then, large: `HE GOETH BEFORE YOU INTO GALILEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back to your ordinary Galilee. Settle and breathe. Your Galilee is the place you spend most of your days. A kitchen, a desk, a car, a classroom, a checkout line. Picture it clearly. Now imagine that someone has gone ahead of you and is already there, waiting, before you arrive tomorrow. Catholics say the risen Christ goes before them into ordinary life. If you pray, you can ask to see him there. If you don't, just picture walking into your ordinary place expecting something good. The bell holds the time.
Risen. What the young man in white tells the frightened women at the empty tomb: he is risen, he is not here. Today's word.
Your line: he goes before you. Tomorrow morning, when you walk into your most ordinary place, pause at the door for one breath before you go in. Day two hundred thirty-one.

myth: the young man's words for the disciples name Peter
"go, tell his disciples and Peter," the one who had denied him.
some of the oldest manuscripts of Mark end with the women afraid and silent
they end at 16:8; later manuscripts add a longer ending, which the Catholic Church receives as Scripture.
the women went to the tomb expecting to see him risen
they brought spices for a body and worried about moving the stone.

fork.setup: you're one of the three women. the stone is rolled back, a young man in white says he is risen, and to go tell the others. what do you do?
options: run and tell everyone right away.
flee, trembling, and say nothing, because you're afraid.
stay and wait inside the tomb.
fork.reveal: "and they said nothing to any man; for they were afraid." in some of the oldest manuscripts, Mark ends right there. clearly, someone spoke eventually.

original.note: Greek: he goes before you, the promise Jesus made on the walk out after supper (14:28).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Easter story, with an ending missing.
what it means: he is risen and has gone ahead to ordinary Galilee, with words for the disciples that name Peter, the one who failed.
what a scholar hears: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8; 16:9–20 is held canonical in Catholic teaching, under Trent's decree on the books 'with all their parts'; proagei echoes 14:28.

sources.ref: Council of Trent, Session 4 (1546), decree on the canonical Scriptures
